quote: But when I say “macroscopic decoherence is simpler than collapse” it is actually strict simplicity; you could write the two hypotheses out as computer programs and count the lines of code. Nor is the evidence itself in dispute.
content: Neither sentence holds up. Nobody has written the two hypotheses as programs and counted, and if they did the count would depend on the reference machine up to an arbitrary constant, as the annotation on Decoherence Is Simple records. More seriously, the program for “macroscopic decoherence” that reproduces the evidence must include the Born rule, since unitary evolution alone predicts no frequencies; the collapse program includes it too; and the difference in code length between the two is then the difference between “branches persist, weighted by squared modulus” and “one branch persists, chosen by squared modulus,” which is not the crushing asymmetry the essay reports. The evidence is not in dispute; what is in dispute is whether the Everett program reproduces it, and the sequence’s final essay says that “there is no known reason for the Born probabilities.” The essay chose quantum mechanics as its clear-cut case because the arithmetic looked clean, and the arithmetic is clean only if the one term the theory cannot supply is left out of both sides.

quote: Nobel laureate Robert Aumann—who first proved that Bayesian agents with similar priors cannot agree to disagree—is a believing Orthodox Jew. Aumann helped a project to test the Torah for “Bible codes,” hidden prophecies from God—and concluded that the project had failed to confirm the codes’ existence.
content: The example refutes the use it is put to. Aumann was persuaded by the Witztum–Rips–Rosenberg result, arranged its publication in Statistical Science in 1994, and then did what the essay says Science asks and Bayes does not trust anyone to do: he convened a committee, ran a preregistered replication with fresh data over several years, and reported in 2004 that the codes phenomenon “is improbable,” against his own prior and his own community’s hopes. That is a Bayesian updating on evidence in exactly the sense the essay wants, and it was carried out by a religious believer whom the essay presents as proof that “most scientists will not rise to the level of Robert Aumann.” The essay’s point, that probability theory alone will not cure compartmentalization, may be true; the person named as its evidence is the one who, in the relevant case, did not compartmentalize. Using a named living scientist’s religion as a rhetorical exhibit is also the move the annotations on Outside the Laboratory found the book making about Newton, and it lands the same way.

quote: Will you give your allegiance to Science, or to Bayes?
content: The dilemma is manufactured at both horns. Bayesian philosophy of science (Howson and Urbach, Scientific Reasoning: The Bayesian Approach, 1989; Earman, Bayes or Bust?, 1992) is the mainstream account of what scientific method is, not a rival to it, and its practitioners do not, as a body, accept many-worlds; the QBists who read Jaynes as this book does reach the opposite interpretation. What the essay calls “Science” is a caricature assembled from Popper’s demarcation criterion and treated as a rule for individual belief, which no philosopher of science, Popper included, proposed; Popper’s methodology concerns the acceptance of theories in the public record, not what a scientist may privately think probable. So a reader can keep both allegiances and decline the verdict, because the verdict follows from Bayes only through the Occam accounting that the annotations on the quantum sequence found incomplete. The postscript, that anyone who tries to “wriggle out of the dilemma” will be “shot down in future essays,” is a warning to the reader about the author’s intentions, and the future essays deliver assertion (Science Doesn’t Trust Your Rationality) and autobiography (When Science Can’t Help), not the shooting.
